overview.title: 📖 Overview: How Far Does Set-Aside Extend for Rabbi Shimon?
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 45a–45b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מוּקְצֶה לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אֶלָּא שֶׁמֶן שֶׁבַּנֵּר בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהוּא דּוֹלֵק, הוֹאִיל וְהוּקְצָה לְמִצְוָתוֹ הוּקְצָה לְאִיסּוּרוֹ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by showing that Rav's own rulings — a lamp placed atop a palm tree before Shabbat but not before a Festival, and the leniency to move a Hanukkah lamp in danger — align him with Rabbi Yehuda's view that set-aside items may not be moved, except under exigent circumstances. Reish Lakish then asks Rabbi Yochanan how far Rabbi Shimon's leniency on set-aside really extends, testing it against sown wheat and incubating eggs. The Gemara pushes this question through sukkah decorations, drying figs and raisins, and unripe dates, before turning to a dispute over wild versus domesticated animals and finally working through several conflicting reports of exactly whose halakha — Rabbi Yehuda's or Rabbi Shimon's — was ultimately accepted.

slides.title: 🌴 A Lamp on a Palm Tree: Shabbat vs. Festival
slides.subtitle: Rav's distinction only makes sense if he follows Rabbi Yehuda

nodes.content: 📜 Rav: one may place a lamp atop a palm tree before Shabbat to burn there, but not before a Festival
❓ If Rav held like Rabbi Shimon (no muktzeh at all), what difference would there be between Shabbat and a Festival?
✅ Since the lamp is set-aside on Shabbat, no one will climb the tree to move it; but since it's movable on a Festival, one might climb up and improperly use the tree itself

callout.label: Objection and answer:
callout.text: Rav permitted moving a Hanukkah lamp away from Persian fire-priests in danger, seemingly against muktzeh — but Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi confirm this was only because 'Rabbi Shimon is worthy to rely on in exigent circumstances.'

slides.title: 🌾 How Far Does Rabbi Shimon's Leniency Go?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish tests the boundary of muktzeh with two hard cases

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Wheat sown in the ground, or eggs placed under a hen to incubate — since one actively rejected them by his own hand, does even Rabbi Shimon agree they're set-aside? Or is there no difference from ordinary cases?

lines.speaker: R. Yochanan
lines.text: There is only one true case of set-aside for Rabbi Shimon: oil in a lamp while it is burning.

lines.speaker: R. Yochanan
lines.text: Since it was set aside for its mitzva — kindling the Shabbat lamp — it is thereby also set aside for its prohibition, the concern of extinguishing it.

callout.label: Immediate challenge:
callout.text: But a baraita forbids using sukkah decorations (nuts, fruit, wreaths) until the festival ends — proof that 'set aside for a mitzva alone' does apply more broadly for Rabbi Shimon.

slides.title: 🎪 Expanding the Cases: Sukkah, Figs, and Dates
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yochanan's statement is refined rather than overturned

boxes.title: Sukkah Decorations
items: Nuts, fruit, and wreaths hung for beauty: forbidden to use until the festival ends
Wood from the sukkah itself: also forbidden (even Rabbi Yehuda agrees here)
Unless the owner stipulated otherwise in advance

boxes.title: Dried Figs & Raisins
items: Shmuel: the only case of set-aside for Rabbi Shimon
One who leaves food on the roof to dry needs prior designation to eat it on Shabbat

boxes.title: Unripe Dates
items: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to his son: still only figs and raisins are muktzeh for Rabbi Shimon
Unripe dates left to ripen are not included

callout.label: Refined rule:
callout.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle is restated: set-aside for Rabbi Shimon applies only in a case 'similar to oil in the lamp' — set aside for its mitzva alone is enough, without any separate Torah prohibition.

slides.title: 🐐 Wild Animals vs. Domesticated Animals
slides.subtitle: A mishna dispute tests whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds any muktzeh at all
headers: May be watered/slaughtered on Yom Tov?
rows: Graze beyond the town limits by day, return to sleep within them
Go out at Passover, return only with the rainy season
Both categories above count as domesticated

callout.label: Three resolutions:
callout.text: Perhaps these animals resemble figs/raisins (an exception even Rabbi Shimon grants); or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi spoke according to Rabbi Shimon without holding it himself; or he spoke within the Rabbis' own framework to win a partial concession.

slides.title: 🏺 Settling the Halakha: Conflicting Reports
slides.subtitle: Several amoraim report Rabbi Yochanan's final ruling differently

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabba bar bar Chana, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: 'They said the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon' — but Rabbi Yochanan himself once ruled strictly about a hen's roost
2️⃣ Resolved: that roost held a dead chick (or an egg laid on Shabbat) — even Rabbi Shimon agrees such items are set aside
3️⃣ Rav Yitzchak son of Rabbi Yosei later reported: Rabbi Yochanan actually ruled like Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled like Rabbi Shimon
4️⃣ Rav Yosef reconciles this: the earlier report ('they said...') meant others said it in Rabbi Yochanan's name — he himself never held that way

callout.label: Supporting evidence:
callout.text: Rabbi Asi, a student of Rabbi Yochanan, would not move a candelabrum that fell on his cloak — consistent with Rabbi Yochanan following Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view.

summary.principle: For Rabbi Shimon, only an item set aside 'like oil in a burning lamp' — for a mitzva that carries its own risk of prohibition — counts as muktzeh; everything else turns out, case by case, to remain permitted, while the final halakhic ruling itself is transmitted in conflicting versions.

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'set aside for its mitzva' is enough to make an item set aside for its prohibition, but only in cases resembling the burning lamp

quiz.q: Why does Rav permit placing a lamp atop a palm tree before Shabbat but not before a Festival?
o: Palm trees are forbidden on Festivals
Since the lamp is muktzeh on Shabbat no one will climb the tree, but since it's movable on a Festival someone might climb up and misuse the tree itself
Lamps cannot burn on Festivals
There is no real distinction
quiz.e: The distinction only makes sense if Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda that the lamp is muktzeh on Shabbat, preventing anyone from climbing to retrieve it; on a Festival where it's movable, climbing the tree becomes a concern.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yochanan's original answer to Reish Lakish, what is the one true case of set-aside (muktzeh) for Rabbi Shimon?
o: Any food left overnight
Oil in a lamp while it is actually burning
Any object touched on Shabbat
Wool that gets wet
quiz.e: Rabbi Yochanan answered that the only case of muktzeh Rabbi Shimon recognizes is oil in a burning lamp, since it was set aside for its mitzva (kindling) and thereby for its prohibition (extinguishing).

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile the sukkah-decorations baraita (forbidding use of hung fruit) with Rabbi Yochanan's statement limiting muktzeh to 'oil in the lamp'?
o: It rejects the sukkah baraita entirely
It refines the statement: muktzeh applies to anything set aside for a mitzva alone, similar in kind to the burning-lamp case, not literally identical to it
It says sukkah decorations were never really forbidden
It concludes Rabbi Shimon has no opinion on sukkot
quiz.e: The Gemara restates Rabbi Yochanan's principle to mean muktzeh applies to anything 'similar to' oil in the lamp — set aside for its mitzva alone is sufficient, resolving the apparent contradiction.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel (in the name of Rav Yehuda), what is the sole case of muktzeh for Rabbi Shimon regarding food left to dry?
o: Any fruit left outside
Dried figs and raisins alone
Only vegetables
Nothing — Rabbi Shimon has no muktzeh at all
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that dried figs and raisins are the only case of muktzeh recognized by Rabbi Shimon, later confirmed to also exclude unripe dates.

quiz.q: How does Rav Yosef reconcile the two conflicting reports about Rabbi Yochanan's final halakhic ruling on set-aside?
o: He says both reports are equally authoritative and unresolved
He explains that the earlier report ('they said the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon') meant others said it in Rabbi Yochanan's name, while Rabbi Yochanan himself actually held like Rabbi Yehuda
He dismisses both reports as unreliable
He says Rabbi Yochanan changed his mind daily
quiz.e: Rav Yosef reads the phrase 'they said' as distancing Rabbi Yochanan from that ruling — implying it was reported by others, while Rabbi Yochanan's own position (per Rav Yitzchak's later report) followed Rabbi Yehuda.
